An initial techno- 2 economic analysis (TEA) was performed at the commencement of the project for a 100,000-tonne-per-year (100TPY) facility. The cost of capture was estimated at $335/tonne (excluding transportation and storage). Key learnings from the initial TEA guided this project. The sorbent performance and the structured sorbent assembly design were found to have the greatest impact on the cost of CO capture. For example, increasing 2 the sorbent capacity and CO adsorption rate reduces the CAPEX contribution to the cost of CO capture. 2 2 Energy requirements could be reduced by minimizing co-adsorption of water on the sorbent and reducing the regeneration temperature, which narrows the temperature range of the thermal swing process. Finally, improving the long-term stability of the sorbent would reduce the sorbent replacement cost, ultimately reducing the OPEX. These sorbent advancements were found to be most crucial to achieving project goals. The results of the initial TEA were used to guide the sorbent screening and structured sorbent design development. Initial Life-cycle Analysis Based on the initial TEA, an initial life-cycle analysis (LCA) was also completed for a 100,000 TPY facility. The LCA revealed that, given the aim of using electrical power for facilitating the thermal regeneration step, the electricity source was the major GHG emissions driver for the overall process. A comparative LCA revealed the significance of the grid mix on the process emissions, and renewables of fossil with carbon capture and storage (CCS) yielded a meaningful negative GHG footprint for the 100,000 TPY facility modeled therein (Table 3). From the initial TEA, the key sorbent performance that drive down the cost of CO removal are low water adsorption, high cyclic stability, and fast kinetics. 2 Reduction of the non-competitive co-adsorption of water ultimately reduces the parasitic energy losses in the regeneration step. Furthermore, sorbent stability is important in reducing structured sorbent replacement frequency and plant downtime. Rapid kinetics reduce the overall cycle duration and can improve CO 2 productivity of a DAC facility.
